strengths: Teacher selection without expensive search is a relevant problem for efficient NLP. The GPT-2/Pythia sweeps and LLaMA experiments provide useful evidence that larger teachers need not produce better students under the examined recipe.

MiniMA shows promising practical results. Table 2 reports improvements on all six benchmarks over the approximately compute-matched ShearedLLaMA baseline, with evaluation covering English, Chinese, reasoning, and coding.

The pruning and distillation objectives are clearly specified. Large-scale training settings, data-mixture statistics, evaluation protocols, and repository/model links support reproducibility, while symmetric student architectures improve compatibility with standard tooling.
weaknesses: The central 2.5× scaling law is insufficiently established. Figures 3–4 do not adequately explain how fixed-student-size optima are selected from the sparsity-grid experiments. Since S approximately equals (1−p)T, selecting points with similar sparsity already produces a nearly linear relationship; the reported R²=0.9957 does not independently validate optimality. Raw comparisons, uncertainty estimates, and held-out predictions across multiple student sizes are needed. This unresolved central claim motivates resubmission next cycle.

Teacher size is confounded with student construction: each student is pruned and initialized from its own teacher, changing architecture, initialization, and pruning severity alongside teacher size. These factors can contribute to the observed degradation. Comparisons using a common student architecture and initialization would better isolate the capacity-gap interpretation. It is also unclear whether the 13B and 70B teachers receive adaptation comparable to the explicitly adapted 7B teacher.

The extrapolation experiments provide limited validation of the coefficient. For a roughly 3B student, finding 7B better than 13B and 70B establishes the best tested teacher, but does not locate an optimum near 2.5× because 7B is the smallest tested LLaMA2 teacher. Likewise, Table 4 changes pruning and distillation methods at one teacher–student size pair; it cannot establish that the optimal ratio remains invariant across those methods.

The compute–performance claim needs revised accounting. Appendix H reports approximately 4.0×10^9 TFLOPs for MiniMA, excluding the 126B-token teacher adaptation in Appendix A. Under the paper's formula, adaptation adds approximately 5.3×10^9 TFLOPs. Figure 5 also relies on explicitly rumored assumptions for some competitors, including Phi and Mistral. Consistent cost boundaries and sensitivity analyses are necessary to substantiate the claimed Pareto frontier.

Reproducibility is weakest for the pilot experiments that establish the main claim. The reduced-token condition is not quantified, and pilot-specific optimization settings and the numerical observations underlying the fit are insufficiently documented. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, leaving the stability of the selected optima unclear.

The secondary instruction-following evidence needs more careful validation. GPT-4 version and answer-order controls, and human-evaluation sample sizes, are unspecified. Appendix L incorrectly interprets Spearman correlation 0.54 as 54% consistency. The coding example praised in Appendix M also incorrectly returns the first array when the second array is empty. These issues weaken confidence in the qualitative capability claims.
